m7-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Correlation, confounding and causal claims”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A shared cause can create an apparent relationship
sections.explanation: Training participation and retention may both relate to other factors. A correlation does not identify an intervention effect or its direction.

items.label: Proposed intervention
items.detail: State the change whose effect you want to understand.

items.label: Observed outcome
items.detail: Define the follow-up result precisely.

items.label: Shared causes
items.detail: Consider workload, role mix or other factors affecting both.

items.label: Selection and direction
items.detail: People may self-select, and the direction of influence can differ.

sections.takeaway: Draw plausible alternative pathways before claiming that changing one variable will change the other.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Association is not an intervention effect

sections.title: Design the comparison before seeing results
sections.explanation: A baseline, outcome window and suitable comparison make the evaluation more informative. Governance and essential support remain constraints.

items.label: Define the outcome
items.detail: Set the population, measure and follow-up in advance.

items.label: Choose a comparison
items.detail: Use an ethical feasible design with explicit assumptions.

items.label: Collect consistently
items.detail: Use the same measurement rules across relevant groups.

items.label: Review the limitations
items.detail: Record remaining differences and missing follow-up.

sections.takeaway: Do not choose only the favourable metric after looking at the data.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Uncertainty should constrain the conclusion
sections.explanation: Small samples, changing conditions and incomplete observation limit what a difference can establish.

items.label: Observed difference
items.detail: Describe what the data actually show.

items.label: Required assumptions
items.detail: State what a causal reading would need.

items.label: Unresolved threats
items.detail: Keep missing data and external changes visible.

items.label: Proportionate decision
items.detail: Recommend more evidence or a bounded test where appropriate.

sections.takeaway: “Promising enough for a better pilot” can be a sound conclusion; statistical adjustment does not erase every bias.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: If trainees stay longer than non-trainees, does that prove training caused retention?
checkpoint.answer: No. Selection, workload, role mix and other factors may explain both. Plan a suitable comparison and state the remaining assumptions and uncertainty.

m7-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Predictive analytics limits and model review”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Read all four cells before quoting accuracy
sections.explanation: The synthetic positive class is “exit” in a fixed teaching evaluation. Four true positives plus 86 true negatives give 90% accuracy, the same as an all-stay baseline.

items.label: True positive · 4
items.detail: Four actual exits were predicted as exits.

items.label: False negative · 6
items.detail: Six actual exits were missed.

items.label: False positive · 4
items.detail: Four stayers were wrongly labelled as exits.

items.label: True negative · 86
items.detail: Eighty-six stayers were predicted as stayers.

sections.takeaway: Precision is 4/(4+4) = 50%; recall is 4/(4+6) = 40%. The aggregate example does not authorise individual employee-risk scoring.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Error types have human consequences
sections.explanation: A threshold trades off errors under a defined evaluation. A score does not explain a person’s intentions.

items.label: False positive
items.detail: Someone could be wrongly labelled or treated differently.

items.label: False negative
items.detail: A real outcome is missed under the model’s rule.

items.label: Threshold choice
items.detail: Review the cost and distribution of mistakes, not only accuracy.

items.label: Human authority
items.detail: Keep consequential decisions under qualified accountable processes.

sections.takeaway: This course uses synthetic aggregate literacy only; do not deploy individual leaver lists or automated adverse actions.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Review time, leakage and operating authority
sections.explanation: A model can look accurate when it uses future information or the same cases for training and evaluation. Performance can also change over time.

items.label: Exclude future knowledge
items.detail: Do not predict exits using fields known only after departure.

items.label: Separate evaluation
items.detail: Use appropriate unseen cases and time boundaries.

items.label: Watch changed conditions
items.detail: Review drift in roles, policy and populations.

items.label: Check authority and remedy
items.detail: Confirm the permitted purpose and route to challenge a consequential result.

sections.takeaway: A vendor score is insufficient: purpose, privacy, fairness, human accountability and contestability need review.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Why is 90% accuracy not a sufficient success claim in the synthetic exit example?
checkpoint.answer: An all-stay baseline also reaches 90% accuracy while detecting no exits. Inspect the confusion matrix, precision, recall, population and human consequences.

m7-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Fairness, disclosure and intervention governance”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A selection disparity is a signal, not a verdict
sections.explanation: The independent synthetic groups have 20 selected of 50 eligible in A and 12 of 40 in B. Counts, role mix and process context still matter.

items.label: Synthetic Group A
items.detail: 20 selected ÷ 50 eligible applicants.

items.label: Synthetic Group B
items.detail: 12 selected ÷ 40 eligible applicants.

sections.takeaway: Rates are 40% and 30%; B/A = 0.75. This is not proof of cause, a legal finding or permission to infer sensitive attributes.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. A disparity is a signal to investigate

sections.title: A screening heuristic is not a law of fairness
sections.explanation: A selection-rate ratio can highlight a question for investigation. One threshold cannot establish universal fairness or legal compliance.

items.label: Check definitions
items.detail: Use eligible comparable populations and an explicit reference.

items.label: Inspect the ratio
items.detail: Show both rates, counts and sample limitations.

items.label: Investigate context
items.detail: Review role mix, criteria, missing data and consequences.

items.label: Escalate appropriately
items.detail: Use authorised qualified reviewers and applicable current requirements.

sections.takeaway: Use qualified HR and legal review for real decisions, not a classroom ratio as a clearance certificate.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Do not turn a heuristic into law

sections.title: Govern the action, not only the metric
sections.explanation: A review needs purpose, alternatives, data authority, affected people and a way to correct or contest errors.

items.label: Define purpose and people
items.detail: Name the use and who could be affected.

items.label: Review alternatives
items.detail: Consider a lower-risk or non-model approach.

items.label: Apply controls
items.detail: Limit data, access, disclosure and consequential actions.

items.label: Review and remedy
items.detail: Assign an owner, correction route and review date.

sections.takeaway: A simpler process improvement may answer the need without any individual scoring.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does a selection-rate ratio above a chosen threshold prove a process is fair and legally compliant?
checkpoint.answer: No. A heuristic is not a universal fairness or Indian legal compliance test. Review definitions, data, context, harms and current requirements with qualified owners.
